As of 227 PM EDT Wednesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: One round of light shower activity has exited east of 
Vermont, and there are some additional light radar returns upstream 
in Canada. Steady, breezy conditions are expected today as northwest 
winds begin to increase overnight. This should allow for some 
continued rounds of light, orographically enhanced showers into. 
Northwesterly flow will result in somewhat cooler air filtering in, 
but the nighttime lows are relatively close to seasonal lows around 
the 30s to lower 40s. Conditions may still be brisk early tomorrow 
morning, but winds show be subsiding by Thursday morning with a cool 
day on tap where we struggle to get much above the 50s beneath 
gradually increasing cloud cover during the afternoon as the next 
system approaches.

KEY MESSAGE 2: For the rain component - Another solid soaker is 
expected for Friday. A digging upper trough and closed mid-level 
cyclone will result in efficient transport of more tropical Pacific 
air. PWATs will surge to around 250-275 percent of normal as a warm 
front begins to approach. Initially, surface conditions will be 
rather dry Thursday night. Still, increasing south flow will result 
in temperatures leveling off after a rather fast initial drop to the 
30s to lower 40s. Confluent low-level flow will bring in some low 
level moisture off the Atlantic. By dawn on Friday, an 850mb jet 
around 45 knots will result in efficient isentropic lift along the 
warm front which will get hung up near or just north of the 
international border. Most likely, precipitation will fall as rain, 
but wet-bulb zero heights are flirting quite close to the ground in 
the Northeast Kingdom with a substantial warm nose overhead. NBM 
probabilities depict 2% snow, but realistically, that would be the 
chance for some wintry mix. Then by afternoon, surface low pressure 
will track through the St. Lawrence Valley. Guidance has the surface 
low track almost overhead, with little time spent in the warm 
sector. We will see temperatures climb into the mid 50s to near 60, 
but that could be a little optimistic. The surface low will shift 
east by Friday night, and then cooler air will quickly filter in 
behind it as a strong 1035mb surface high builds to our west.

For the wind component - The wind forecast is somewhat challenging. 
On one hand, the low-level jet is strong, but it appears most likely 
to be raining when it peaks, and forecast soundings depict the jet 
above the bottom of the inversion layer. It seems most likely that 
the strongest winds will come from channeled flow with the highest 
gusts of 30-40 mph in and around Lake Champlain for Friday morning. 
Winds will briefly dip as surface low pressure tracks over the 
region during the day, and then wind speeds will ramp up due to the 
increasing pressure gradient from the strong 1035mb surface high. 
Widespread 25 to 35 mph gusts will persist Friday night into early 
Saturday as temperatures cool. This will make for a chilly night as 
temperatures fall into the mid 20s to mid 30s. Apparent temps/wind 
chills will reach the teens in higher elevations and lower 20s in 
the broader valleys for Saturday morning.

For the snow shower component - With temperatures falling into the 
mid 20s to mid 30s range, that means we get to talk snow. Low-level 
moisture is expected to linger into midday Saturday. With the 
persistent northwest flow, orographic lift is expected for our 
northwest facing mountains. Snow levels appear like they could make 
it near the valley floors, but high froude values and incoming dry 
air will generally favor accumulations above 1500 ft agl. So even as 
far down as Burlington could feasibly observe snow, but it's more 
likely to be just a quick dusting for the Adirondacks, Northeast 
Kingdom, and summits of the Green Mountains. Snowfall amounts for 
these areas will be generally 1" or less, but 2" could feasibly 
occur atop mountain peaks above 3000 ft.

potential for developing southeast CONUS ridge to expand into the 
Mid Atlantic/NE CONUS by early next week. This large scale synoptic 
pattern supports temps trending above normal levels by early next 
week with mostly dry conditions prevailing. We can never completely 
rule out a weak embedded short wave in the fast zonal flow aloft,
